The topology of projective codes
and the distribution of zeros of odd mapsThanks: FF was supported by NSF grant DMS 1855591 and a Sloan Research Fellowship.

Henry Adams HADepartment of Mathematics, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO 80523, USA Email address: henry.adams@colostate.edu , Johnathan Bush JBDepartment of Mathematics, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611, USA Email address: bush.j@ufl.edu and Florian Frick FFDept. Math. Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA
Inst. Math., Freie Universität Berlin, Arnimallee 2, 14195 Berlin, Germany Email address: frick@cmu.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We show that the size of codes in projective space controls structural results for zeros of odd maps from spheres to Euclidean space. In fact, this relation is given through the topology of the space of probability measures on the sphere whose supports have diameter bounded by some specific parameter. Our main result is a generalization of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem, and we derive four consequences of it: (i) We give a new proof of a result of Simonyi and Tardos on topological lower bounds for the circular chromatic number of a graph; (ii) we study generic embeddings of spheres into Euclidean space and show that projective codes give quantitative bounds for a measure of genericity of sphere embeddings; and we prove generalizations of (iii) the Ham Sandwich theorem and (iv) the Lyusternik–Shnirel’man–Borsuk covering theorem for the case where the number of measures or sets in a covering, respectively, may exceed the ambient dimension.

Key words and phrases: 
Projective codes, Borsuk–Ulam theorems, metric thickenings
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
52C17, 55N91, 05B40, 55N31.

1. Introduction

Given a compact metric space (X,d)(X,d), a central problem in coding theory is to determine a configuration of nn points in XX that maximizes the minimal distance between them. More precisely, for each n≥1n\geq 1, we define

pn(X)≔sup{ε>0:there arex1,…,xn∈Xwithd(xi,xj)≥εfor alli≠j}.p_{n}(X)\coloneqq\sup\{\varepsilon>0~:~\text{there are}\ x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in X\ \text{with}\ d(x_{i},x_{j})\geq\varepsilon\ \text{for all}\ i\neq j\}.

By compactness, one can find {x1,…,xn}⊆X\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\subseteq X such that d⁡(xi,xj)≥pn​(X)d(x_{i},x_{j})\geq p_{n}(X) whenever i≠ji\neq j; such a set is called a code of size nn.

For the dd-sphere SdS^{d}, a code {x1,…,xn}⊂Sd\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\subset S^{d} is called a spherical code. Spherical codes have generated considerable interest; see for example [44].

Spheres are naturally equipped with the ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action exchanging antipodal points, denoted x↦−xx\mapsto-x, and a subset of a sphere that is invariant under this action is said to be centrally-symmetric. Hence, one may also consider the problem of finding centrally-symmetric spherical codes, that is, spherical codes in which points come in antipodal pairs {x,−x}\{x,-x\} [13, 16]. By equipping real projective space ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d} with the quotient metric induced by the antipodal action, a centrally-symmetric spherical code in SdS^{d} is equivalent to a code in ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d}, i.e. a projective code. With this metric, the distance between two points in ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d} is the angle between the lines they determine in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}. In other words, a projective code is a collection of lines through the origin in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} that are as close to orthogonal as possible. Therefore, the problem of finding a projective code of size nn may be rephrased as follows: Given c>0c>0, find nn unit vectors x1,…,xn∈Sd⊂ℝd+1x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in S^{d}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1} such that |⟨xi,xj⟩|≤c|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\leq c whenever i≠ji\neq j.

In the present manuscript, we establish relationships between projective codes and the following two problem areas:

  1. (1)

    Metric thickenings: For a compact metric space XX and δ>0\delta>0, determine bounds for the topology of the space of probability measures on XX supported on finite sets of diameter at most δ\delta, equipped with an optimal transport metric. This is the metric thickening XδX_{\delta} at scale δ\delta.

  2. (2)

    Zeros of odd maps: A map f:Sd→ℝf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is odd if f⁡(−x)=−f⁡(x)f(-x)=-f(x) for all x∈Sdx\in S^{d}. Let VV be an nn-dimensional vector space of continuous odd maps Sd→ℝS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}. Find a small δ≥0\delta\geq 0 such that there is a set A⊂SdA\subset S^{d} of diameter at most δ\delta with the property that for every f∈Vf\in V the restriction f|Af|_{A} is not strictly positive.

Metric thickenings were introduced in [2] to capture the geometry of a metric space at a given scale δ>0{\delta>0}. Here we show that large projective codes provide lower bounds for the topology of metric thickenings of spheres (in terms of their cohomological index), which in turn give non-trivial upper bounds for δ\delta in problem area (2), and thus structural results for zeros of odd maps. Our main result is:

Theorem 1.

Let VV be an nn-dimensional vector space of continuous odd maps Sd→ℝS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}. Then there is a set A⊂SdA\subset S^{d} of diameter at most δ=π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta=\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) such that for every f∈Vf\in V the restriction f|Af|_{A} is not strictly positive.

Thus if ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d} has a close packing by metric balls, then odd maps Sd→ℝS^{d}\to\mathbb{R} cannot stay positive on large subsets of SdS^{d}. One can regard Theorem 1 as an asymptotic Borsuk–Ulam theorem. To recover the classical Borsuk–Ulam theorem that any odd map Sn→ℝnS^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} has a zero, one must instead phrase Theorem 1 in terms of the topology of metric thickenings of the sphere; see Remark 3.1. This theorem improves on a recent Borsuk–Ulam result for odd maps Sd→ℝnS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} with n≥dn\geq d, proven by the authors in [3]. We also refer the reader to [17], which uses characteristic classes to give related generalizations of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem into higher-dimensional codomains. The Borsuk–Ulam theorem has found numerous applications across mathematics; see for instance [35] for applications in combinatorics and discrete geometry.

An equivalent formulation of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem states that there does not exist a continuous odd map Sn→SdS^{n}\to S^{d} when n>dn>d. However, the obstruction to the existence of such maps can be eliminated by thickening the codomain. The following theorem makes this precise and establishes a relationship between the topology of metric thickenings of spheres and projective codes.

Theorem 2.

Let dd and nn be positive integers, and let δ≥π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta\geq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}). Then there is a continuous odd map Sn→SδdS^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta}.

Theorem 2 gives lower bounds for the topology of metric thickenings of spheres, SδdS^{d}_{\delta}, in terms of packings of metric balls in projective space. Dually, coverings of projective space by metric balls provide upper bounds for the topology of metric thickenings in Theorem 3. Thus the topology of the metric thickening SδdS^{d}_{\delta} is sandwiched between packings and coverings of projective space.

Theorem 3.

Let δ>0\delta>0. Suppose there are nn points x1,…,xn∈ℝ​Pdx_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathbb{R}P^{d} such that every point y∈ℝ​Pdy\in\mathbb{R}P^{d} is strictly within distance δ\delta from one of the xjx_{j}. Then there is an odd map Sπ−2​δd→Sn−1S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta}\to S^{n-1}.

The following result about odd maps from metric thickenings into spheres, when combined with Theorem 2, implies Theorem 1; see Section 3 for the proof.

Theorem 4.

Let XX be a metric space with a free ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action, and let δ>0\delta>0. Let VV be an nn-dimensional real vector space of continuous odd functions f:X→ℝf\colon X\to\mathbb{R}, such that for every A⊂XA\subset X of diameter at most δ\delta there is an f∈Vf\in V such that f|Af|_{A} is strictly positive. Then there is an odd map Xδ→Sn−1X_{\delta}\to S^{n-1}.

After proving the results outlined above, we will derive applications of Theorem 1. Some of these are generalizations of the familiar consequences of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem, while others are new applications that require the added generality of Theorem 1 to produce interesting results. Applications of the latter kind are the following:

  1. (i)

    A well-studied problem concerns generic manifold embeddings, that is, if a manifold MM embeds into ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, does it embed in a particularly generic way, for example, such that tangent lines at different points are skew [20] or non-parallel [27], or such that any kk pairwise distinct points map to linearly independent points [10]. Here we show that for embeddings of spheres into ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} a notion of genericity of embeddings is governed by the size of projective codes; see Section 4.

  2. (ii)

    Simonyi and Tardos [42] established topological lower bounds for the circular chromatic number of a graph in terms of the topology of its box complex. Theorem 1 is already interesting in the case d=1d=1 of the circle S1S^{1}, where we derive the Simonyi–Tardos result as a consequence, thereby giving a new proof of their result that provides new insights into why topological bounds of the circular chromatic number depend on the parity of the coindex of the box complex; see Section 5.

For two of the usual consequences of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem, we prove generalizations to possibly “overdetermined” cases. These consequences are:

  1. (iii)

    The Ham Sandwich theorem asserts that any dd continuous probability measures on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} can be simultaneously bisected by an affine hyperplane. We prove a generalization of this result to the case of n≥dn\geq d probability measures, where we have to relax the notion of bisection; see Section 6.

  2. (iv)

    In any covering of SnS^{n} by n+1n+1 closed sets, one of these sets contains a pair of antipodal points. We generalize this result by showing that this remains true for coverings of SnS^{n} by more than n+1n+1 sets, provided that every subset of SnS^{n} of a certain diameter appears in at least one of those sets; see Section 7.

2. Context

We begin with some preliminary material, definitions, and lemmas.

2.1. Structural results for zeros of odd maps

Let XX and YY be spaces with ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-actions, that is, both XX and YY are equipped with a continuous involution, which we will denote x↦−xx\mapsto-x for x∈Xx\in X and similarly y↦−yy\mapsto-y for y∈Yy\in Y. For the sphere SdS^{d} and for Euclidean space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} we always fix the antipodal ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action. We will refer to any ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-equivariant map f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y (i.e., f⁡(−x)=−f⁡(x)f(-x)=-f(x) for all x∈Xx\in X) as an odd map. The central result about zeros of odd maps is the Borsuk–Ulam theorem [11]:

Theorem 5.

Any continuous odd map f:Sd→ℝdf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} has a zero. Equivalently, there is no continuous odd map Sd→Sd−1S^{d}\to S^{d-1}.

Bourgin [12, Theorem 4A] and Yang [45] proved generalizations of this theorem asserting that for any continuous odd map f:Sd→ℝnf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} with 1≤n≤d1\leq n\leq d, the preimage f−1​(0)f^{-1}(0) contains an antipodally symmetric (d−n)(d-n)-dimensional cycle, which when mapped into the corresponding projective space ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d}, is a non-zero element of Hd−n​(ℝ​Pd,ℤ/2)H_{d-n}(\mathbb{R}P^{d};\mathbb{Z}/2). From Theorem 1 we can derive a Borsuk–Ulam theorem for the complementary case n>dn>d, as explained in Section 4. This improves on an earlier result of the authors in [3] that bridges applied, quantitative, and equivariant topology.

To explain the connection between Borsuk–Ulam theorems and projective codes, we say that a set Y⊂ℝnY\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a Carathéodory subset if its convex hull captures the origin in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, i.e. if 0∈conv⁡(Y)0\in\mathrm{conv}(Y). In particular, any set YY that contains antipodal points y0,−y0∈Yy_{0},-y_{0}\in Y, such as the image of an odd map f:Sd→ℝnf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, is trivially a Carathéodory subset. While the image of a continuous odd map f:Sd→ℝnf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} may miss the origin, we will explain in Section 4 how Theorem 2 implies that for some set A⊂SdA\subset S^{d} of diameter strictly less than π\pi, the restricted image f⁡(A)f(A) is still a Carathéodory subset.

In order to recover the topological lower bounds for the circular chromatic number of a graph due to Simonyi and Tardos [42] in Section 5, we will need an auxiliary result from [3]: Let

SM2​k​(t)=(cos⁡t,sin⁡t,cos⁡(3​t),sin⁡(3​t),…,cos⁡((2​k−1)​t),sin⁡((2​k−1)​t))\mathrm{SM}_{2k}(t)=\left(\cos t,\sin t,\cos(3t),\sin(3t),\dots,\cos((2k-1)t),\sin((2k-1)t)\right)

be the symmetric trigonometric moment curve. We may think of SM2​k\mathrm{SM}_{2k} as a map S1→ℝ2​kS^{1}\to\mathbb{R}^{2k} under the identification S1=ℝ/2​π​ℤS^{1}=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}, with the antipodal action specified by t↦t+πt\mapsto t+\pi. Observe that SM2​k\mathrm{SM}_{2k} is an odd map. Furthermore, the preimage of any Carathéodory subset of the image of SM2​k\mathrm{SM}_{2k} must have sufficiently large diameter in the circle S1S^{1}:

Lemma 2.1 ([3, Theorem 5]).

Let X⊂S1X\subset S^{1} be a set with diameter strictly less than 2​π​k2​k+1\frac{2\pi k}{2k+1}. Then the convex hull of SM2​k​(X)\mathrm{SM}_{2k}(X) does not contain the origin.

For example, in the case k=1k=1, Lemma 2.1 reduces to the statement that no subset of S1⊂ℝ2S^{1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} of diameter less than 2​π3\frac{2\pi}{3} can contain the origin in its convex hull; this is Jung’s Theorem in the plane [29, Lemma 2]. This lemma can be seen as a structural result for zeros of raked trigonometric polynomials; see [3, Theorem 4]. We will need the following consequence of Lemma 2.1 in Section 5:

Lemma 2.2.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 be an integer and let δ<2​π​k2​k+1\delta<\frac{2\pi k}{2k+1}. Then there is a continuous odd map f:Sδ1→S2​k−1f\colon S^{1}_{\delta}\to S^{2k-1}.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1 the map SM2​k:S1→ℝ2​k\mathrm{SM}_{2k}\colon S^{1}\to\mathbb{R}^{2k} extends linearly to an odd map f^:Sδ1→ℝ2​k∖{0}\widehat{f}\colon S^{1}_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{2k}\setminus\{0\}. Then f⁡(x)=f^​(x)‖f^​(x)‖f(x)=\frac{\widehat{f}(x)}{\|\widehat{f}(x)\|} is the desired map. ∎

The bound on δ\delta in Lemma 2.2 is optimal: there is a homotopy equivalence Sδ1≃S2​k+1S^{1}_{\delta}\simeq S^{2k+1} for 2​π​k2​k+1≤δ<2​π​(k+1)2​k+3\frac{2\pi k}{2k+1}\leq\delta<\frac{2\pi(k+1)}{2k+3} [39, 1], which can furthermore be made ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-equivariant.

2.2. Cohomological index

Observe that Theorems 2, 3, and 4 are statements regarding the existence of continuous odd maps into and out of spheres. Results along these lines are commonly phrased in terms of the cohomological index, which we now recall.

Let XX be a metric space with a free ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action, that is, a fixed-point free involution. Let S∞=∪n=0∞SnS^{\infty}=\cup_{n=0}^{\infty}S^{n}, where each SnS^{n} is the equator of Sn+1S^{n+1}. Up to ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-equivariant homotopy (i.e., a homotopy that at every time commutes with the ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action) there is a unique odd map X→S∞X\to S^{\infty}, which gives X/(ℤ/2)→ℝ​P∞X/(\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathbb{R}P^{\infty} on quotients. This induces a map H∗​(ℝ​P∞,𝔽2)→H∗​(X/(ℤ/2),𝔽2)H^{*}(\mathbb{R}P^{\infty};\mathbb{F}_{2})\to H^{*}(X/(\mathbb{Z}/2);\mathbb{F}_{2}) in cohomology with 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-coefficients, where H∗​(ℝ​P∞,𝔽2)≅𝔽2​[t]H^{*}(\mathbb{R}P^{\infty};\mathbb{F}_{2})\cong\mathbb{F}_{2}[t]. The smallest integer nn such that tn+1t^{n+1} is in the kernel of this map is the cohomological index (or Stiefel–Whitney height) of XX and denoted by ind⁡(X)\mathrm{ind}(X); see [35]. If there is an odd map X→SnX\to S^{n}, then ind⁡(X)≤n\mathrm{ind}(X)\leq n. On the other hand, if there is an odd map Sn→XS^{n}\to X then n≤ind⁡(X)n\leq\mathrm{ind}(X). We refer to the largest nn such that there is an odd map Sn→XS^{n}\to X as the coindex of XX, denoted by coind⁡(X)\mathrm{coind}(X), which by the previous sentence satisfies coind⁡(X)≤ind⁡(X)\mathrm{coind}(X)\leq\mathrm{ind}(X).

2.3. Metric thickenings

Let (X,d)(X,d) be a metric space and let δ≥0\delta\geq 0. The (Vietoris–Rips) metric thickening XδX_{\delta} of XX at scale δ\delta is the set of probability measures μ\mu in XX whose support supp⁡(μ)\mathrm{supp}(\mu) is finite and has diameter at most δ\delta, equipped with the 11-Wasserstein metric of optimal transport. See [2] for an introduction. In particular, we can write elements μ∈Xδ\mu\in X_{\delta} as convex combinations μ=∑k=1nλi​xi\mu=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}x_{i}, where λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0, ∑i=1nλi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}=1, and x1,…,xn∈Xx_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in X with d⁡(xi,xj)≤δd(x_{i},x_{j})\leq\delta for all 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n; see Figure 1. Here we identify each point xi∈Xx_{i}\in X with the Dirac measure at xix_{i}. Notice that in this way XX is naturally a subspace of XδX_{\delta}, embedded isometrically.

Originally, metric thickenings were defined to introduce tools from metric geometry to the study of Vietoris–Rips complexes, that is, the simplicial complex VR⁡(X,δ)\mathrm{VR}(X;\delta) of all finite subsets of XX of diameter at most δ\delta. These complexes are ubiquitous in computational topology and topological data analysis [15]. Despite their prevalence in these areas, the topology of Vietoris–Rips complexes and thickenings is not well-understood, unless the scale parameter δ\delta is small [28, 30, 2] or the underlying metric space XX is simple [1, 39]. See [4, 5, 38] for relationships between Vietoris–Rips complexes and Vietoris–Rips metric thickenings in the context of applied topology. Because metric thickenings parametrize the collection of subsets of a metric space of bounded diameter, they are the correct “configuration space” for studying such subsets. Indeed, the topology of metric thickenings of spheres SδdS_{\delta}^{d} will play a key role in the proofs of our main results.

The choice to restrict the metric thickening XδX_{\delta} to probability measures supported in finitely many points is essentially immaterial; this restriction is the easiest way to ensure that the 11-Wasserstein distance between such measures is well-defined. (Otherwise we could instead require that every probability measure on XX is inner regular, that is, for each open U⊂XU\subset X the measure μ⁡(U)\mu(U) can be approximated arbitrarily closely by μ⁡(C)\mu(C), where C⊂UC\subset U is compact.) Also, one could instead choose to equip the metric thickening XδX_{\delta} with the qq-Wasserstein metric for any q∈[1,∞)q\in[1,\infty).

Any map f:X→ℝnf\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^{n} induces a natural map f:Xδ→ℝnf\colon X_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} by f⁡(μ)=∫Xf​𝑑μf(\mu)=\int_{X}f\ d\mu, where for μ=∑λi​xi\mu=\sum\lambda_{i}x_{i} the integral ∫Xf​𝑑μ\int_{X}f\ d\mu is simply the sum ∑λi​f​(xi)\sum\lambda_{i}f(x_{i}). The extended map on XδX_{\delta} is also denoted ff, since no confusion can arise: The value of f⁡(x)f(x) for x∈Xx\in X does not depend on whether we interpret xx as a point in XX or the Dirac measure centered at xx. We call this naturally extended map f:Xδ→ℝnf\colon X_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} the linear extension of ff, and say that ff was linearly extended. If f:X→ℝnf\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is continuous and bounded, then its linear extension f:Xδ→ℝnf\colon X_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is continuous [2, Lemma 5.2].

Suppose XX is equipped with a ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action. Then the generator of ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2 defines an involution ι:X→X\iota\colon X\to X. This extends to an involution ι:Xδ→Xδ\iota\colon X_{\delta}\to X_{\delta} in a natural way: ι⁡(∑λi​xi)=∑λi​ι​(xi)\iota(\sum\lambda_{i}x_{i})=\sum\lambda_{i}\iota(x_{i}). Thus XδX_{\delta} is a ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-space as well. If the action on XX is free, then the induced action on XδX_{\delta} is free as well, provided that d⁡(x,ι⁡(x))>δd(x,\iota(x))>\delta for all x∈Xx\in X.

3. The cohomological index of metric thickenings

We will first prove lower bounds for the topology of metric thickenings in terms of the size of projective codes. These lower bounds are in terms of the coindex of metric thickenings. Algebraically, this is approximately captured by the (integer-valued ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-)cohomological index; see Section 2.2 for a brief introduction. For convenience, we restate these theorems from the introduction before giving the proofs; note that we now also refer to the cohomological index of a space.

Theorem 2.

Let dd and nn be positive integers, and let δ≥π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta\geq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}). Then there is a continuous odd map Sn→SδdS^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta}; in particular, n≤coind⁡(Sδd)≤ind⁡(Sδd)n\leq\mathrm{coind}(S^{d}_{\delta})\leq\mathrm{ind}(S^{d}_{\delta}).

Proof.

We will construct an odd map f:Sn→Sδdf\colon S^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta}. Let α=pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\alpha=p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}). By compactness, we can find x1,…,xn+1∈ℝ​Pdx_{1},\dots,x_{n+1}\in\mathbb{R}P^{d} that are pairwise at distance at least α\alpha. Each xjx_{j} lifts to two points xj−x_{j}^{-} and xj+x_{j}^{+} in SdS^{d}. These points are antipodes at distance π\pi, but the distance to any other point xi±x_{i}^{\pm} for i≠ji\neq j is at most π−α\pi-\alpha. Indeed, the point xi±x_{i}^{\pm} lies on a shortest path connecting xj+x_{j}^{+} to xj−x_{j}^{-}. Since its distance to xj−x_{j}^{-} is at least α\alpha, it is within a distance of π−α\pi-\alpha from xj+x_{j}^{+}. Symmetrically, since its distance to xj+x_{j}^{+} is at least α\alpha, it is within a distance of π−α\pi-\alpha from xj−x_{j}^{-}.

We will think of the domain of the odd map f:Sn→Sδdf\colon S^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta} as the ℓ1\ell_{1} unit sphere in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, that is, as the boundary of the (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional crosspolytope with vertices ±e1,…,±en+1\pm e_{1},\dots,\pm e_{n+1}. Define ff on vertices by mapping ±ej\pm e_{j} to the Dirac measure at xj±x_{j}^{\pm}. Then extend linearly, that is, given a point ∑i=1n+1λi​εi​ei\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}e_{i} in the ℓ1\ell_{1} unit sphere for some choice of signs εi∈{−1,1}\varepsilon_{i}\in\{-1,1\} and coefficients λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0 with ∑i=1n+1λi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_{i}=1, define f⁡(∑i=1n+1λi​εi​ei)=∑i=1n+1λi​εi​f​(ei)f(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}e_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}f(e_{i}). This is a measure supported on at most n+1n+1 points whose pairwise distances are at most π−α≤δ\pi-\alpha\leq\delta. ∎

The proof above shows that a projective code x1,…,xn+1∈ℝ​Pdx_{1},\dots,x_{n+1}\in\mathbb{R}P^{d}, where any two points are at distance at least α\alpha, induces a linear map from the boundary of the (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional crosspolytope Sn→SδdS^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta} for δ≥π−α\delta\geq\pi-\alpha. Here SδdS^{d}_{\delta} is a subset of the vector space of signed measures on SdS^{d}, so linearity is well-defined. Conversely, any map Sn→SδdS^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta} that is linear in this sense induces a projective code, where elements are at distance at least π−δ\pi-\delta. The cohomological index of SδdS^{d}_{\delta} provides an algebraic witness for the existence of odd maps Sn→SδdS^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta}, and thus the parametrized family of cohomological indices of SδdS^{d}_{\delta} as δ\delta ranges over (0,π)(0,\pi) is a topological version of projective codes.

As remarked in the introduction, coverings of projective space by metric balls dually provide upper bounds for the topology of metric thickenings; see Theorem 3. In other words, simple volume bounds for the size of projective codes apply more generally to bound the topology of metric thickenings. A collection of nn metric δ\delta-balls in ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d} cannot be pairwise disjoint if the sum of their volumes exceeds the volume of ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d}. This bound for projective codes applies more generally as an upper bound for the topology of metric thickenings of spheres.

Theorem 3.

Let δ>0\delta>0. Suppose there are nn points x1,…,xn∈ℝ​Pdx_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathbb{R}P^{d} such that every point y∈ℝ​Pdy\in\mathbb{R}P^{d} is strictly within distance δ\delta from one of the xjx_{j}. Then there is an odd map Sπ−2​δd→Sn−1S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta}\to S^{n-1}; in particular, ind⁡(Sπ−2​δd)≤n−1\mathrm{ind}(S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta})\leq n-1.

Proof.

We think of each xj∈ℝ​Pdx_{j}\in\mathbb{R}P^{d} as a pair of antipodal points ±xj\pm x_{j} in SdS^{d}. If y∈Sdy\in S^{d} has distance less than δ\delta from xjx_{j} and z∈Sdz\in S^{d} has distance less than δ\delta from −xj-x_{j}, then yy and zz are at a distance exceeding π−2​δ\pi-2\delta. Thus for any μ∈Sπ−2​δd\mu\in S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta} the support of μ\mu does not intersect both Bδ​(xj)B_{\delta}(x_{j}) and Bδ​(−xj)B_{\delta}(-x_{j}). Let fj:Sπ−2​δd→ℝf_{j}\colon S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta}\to\mathbb{R} be the map that for μ∈Sπ−2​δd\mu\in S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta} with support disjoint from Bδ​(−xj)B_{\delta}(-x_{j}) is defined as

inf{d(μ,ν):ν∈Sπd,supp(ν)∩Bδ(xj)=∅},\inf\{d(\mu,\nu)~:~\nu\in S^{d}_{\pi},\ \mathrm{supp}(\nu)\cap B_{\delta}(x_{j})=\emptyset\},

where the distance between measures is the 1-Wasserstein distance. Extend this map to all of Sπ−2​δdS^{d}_{\pi-2\delta} by declaring that fj​(−μ)=−fj​(μ)f_{j}(-\mu)=-f_{j}(\mu). It is easily verified that this is a well-defined, continuous odd map. The map f:Sπ−2​δd→ℝnf\colon S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} given by f=(f1,…,fn)f=(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) is odd and misses the origin. Thus μ↦f⁡(μ)‖f⁡(μ)‖\mu\mapsto\frac{f(\mu)}{\|f(\mu)\|} is an odd map Sπ−2​δd→Sn−1S^{d}_{\pi-2\delta}\to S^{n-1}. ∎

The next theorem, when combined with Theorem 2, will allow us to prove our main result, Theorem 1.

Theorem 4.

Let XX be a metric space with a free ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action, and let δ>0\delta>0. Let VV be an nn-dimensional real vector space of continuous odd functions f:X→ℝf\colon X\to\mathbb{R}, such that for every A⊂XA\subset X of diameter at most δ\delta there is an f∈Vf\in V such that f|Af|_{A} is strictly positive. Then there is an odd map Xδ→Sn−1X_{\delta}\to S^{n-1}; in particular, ind⁡(Xδ)≤n−1\mathrm{ind}(X_{\delta})\leq n-1.

Proof.

Fix a basis BB of VV, so |B|=n|B|=n. For μ∈Xδ\mu\in X_{\delta} and f∈Vf\in V let f⁡(μ)=∫Xf​𝑑μf(\mu)=\int_{X}f\ d\mu. Define Φ:Xδ→ℝn\Phi\colon X_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} by Φ⁡(μ)=(f⁡(μ))f∈B\Phi(\mu)=(f(\mu))_{f\in B}. Every element of VV is a linear combination of BB and thus a function of the form x↦⟨z,Φ⁡(x)⟩x\mapsto\langle z,\Phi(x)\rangle for some z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Here xx denotes the Dirac measure δx\delta_{x}. Let μ∈Xδ\mu\in X_{\delta} be arbitrary, and denote its support by AA. There is some f∈Vf\in V such that f|Af|_{A} is strictly positive. Thus ⟨z,Φ⁡(x)⟩>0\langle z,\Phi(x)\rangle>0 for some z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and every x∈Ax\in A. In particular, ⟨z,Φ⁡(μ)⟩>0\langle z,\Phi(\mu)\rangle>0 and thus Φ\Phi maps to ℝn∖{0}≃Sn−1\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}\simeq S^{n-1}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.

Let VV be an nn-dimensional vector space of continuous odd maps Sd→ℝS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}. We must show that there is a set A⊂SdA\subset S^{d} of diameter at most δ:=π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta:=\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) such that for every f∈Vf\in V the restriction f|Af|_{A} is not strictly positive.

Theorem 2 implies ind⁡(Sδd)≥n\mathrm{ind}(S^{d}_{\delta})\geq n. If there were no such set A⊂SdA\subset S^{d}, then for all sets of diameter at most δ\delta there would be some f∈Vf\in V such that the restriction f|Af|_{A} is strictly positive, so Theorem 4 would imply ind⁡(Sδd)≤n−1\mathrm{ind}(S^{d}_{\delta})\leq n-1, a contradiction. ∎

Remark 3.1.

Instead of δ=π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta=\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) we could have phrased Theorem 1 for the smallest δ\delta such that the metric thickening SδdS^{d}_{\delta} has cohomological index at least nn, i.e., such that ind⁡(Sδd)≥n\mathrm{ind}(S^{d}_{\delta})\geq n. For n=dn=d, this δ\delta is zero, since SdS^{d} is a subspace of SδdS^{d}_{\delta} for any δ≥0\delta\geq 0. In the case n=dn=d and δ=0\delta=0, this stronger version of Theorem 1 says that given any dd-dimensional vector space VV of continuous odd maps Sd→ℝS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}, there is a point x∈Sdx\in S^{d} (i.e., a set of diameter zero) such that f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0 (since f∈Vf\in V implies −f∈V-f\in V) for all f∈Vf\in V. By choosing VV to be generated by the dd coordinate functions of an odd map g:Sd→ℝdg\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, we hence obtain the standard Borsuk–Ulam Theorem stating there exists some x∈Sdx\in S^{d} with g⁡(x)=0g(x)=0.

To conclude this section, we give an example of explicit bounds that may be derived from Theorem 2. For general upper and lower bounds for the size of projective codes, see Levenshtein [31]. For our explicit example, we are interested in projective codes whose size exceeds the dimension by a fixed integer. Bukh and Cox [13] study the behaviour of pd+k​(ℝ​Pd)p_{d+k}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) for fixed kk as dd grows. Among other results they show:

Theorem 6 (Bukh and Cox [13], Theorem 21).

Let k≥1k\geq 1 be an integer. Then

pd−1+k​(ℝ​Pd−1)≥arccos⁡((1+o⁡(1))​2​k+1d),p_{d-1+k}(\mathbb{R}P^{d-1})\geq\arccos\left((1+o(1))\frac{2\sqrt{k+1}}{d}\right),

where o⁡(1)o(1) denotes a function that converges to 00 as d→∞d\to\infty.

By combining Theorem 6 with Theorem 2, we immediately get the following consequence for the topology of Vietoris–Rips metric thickenings of spheres:

Corollary 3.2.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 be an integer and δ>π2\delta>\frac{\pi}{2}. Then for d=d⁡(k,δ)d=d(k,\delta) sufficiently large, there is a continuous odd map Sd+k→SδdS^{d+k}\to S^{d}_{\delta}. Indeed, we need to choose dd sufficiently large such that δ>π−arccos⁡((1+o⁡(1))​2​k+2d+1)\delta>\pi-\arccos\left((1+o(1))\frac{2\sqrt{k+2}}{d+1}\right), where o⁡(1)o(1) denotes a function that converges to 00 as d→∞d\to\infty.

Proof.

By Theorem 6 we have pd+k+1​(ℝ​Pd)≥arccos⁡((1+o⁡(1))​2​k+2d+1)→π2p_{d+k+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d})\geq\arccos\left((1+o(1))\frac{2\sqrt{k+2}}{d+1}\right)\to\frac{\pi}{2} as d→∞d\to\infty. So for δ>π2\delta>\frac{\pi}{2} we have δ≥π−pd+k+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta\geq\pi-p_{d+k+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) for dd sufficiently large, in which case Theorem 2 gives an odd map Sd+k→SδdS^{d+k}\to S^{d}_{\delta}. ∎

For δ≤π2\delta\leq\frac{\pi}{2} we have that Sδd≃SdS^{d}_{\delta}\simeq S^{d} [2]. Corollary 3.2 asserts that for any δ>π2\delta>\frac{\pi}{2}, there is an arbitrarily large jump in coindex between Sπ/2dS^{d}_{\pi/2} and SδdS^{d}_{\delta} for dd sufficiently large.

4. Convexity properties of odd maps and generic manifold embeddings

The fundamental result about zeros of odd maps is the classical Borsuk–Ulam theorem: Any continuous odd map Sd→ℝdS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} has a zero, or equivalently, any continuous map f:Sd→ℝdf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} identifies two antipodal points, f⁡(−x)=f⁡(x)f(-x)=f(x). Generalizations of this result that quantify the size of the zero set or preimage of a point for maps Sd→ℝnS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} for n≤dn\leq d were proven by Bourgin [12], Yang [45, 46], Almgren [7], and Gromov [22, 23, 25, 37]. Our Theorem 1 studies an approximate Borsuk–Ulam result for maps Sd→ℝnS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} in which we instead have n≥dn\geq d.

To explain this connection, recall from Section 2.1 that we say a set Y⊂ℝnY\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a Carathéodory subset if its convex hull captures the origin, 0∈conv⁡(Y)0\in\mathrm{conv}(Y). Any set that contains antipodal points, such as the image of an odd map Sd→ℝnS^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, is trivially a Carathéodory subset. We will explain how Theorem 2 shows that for some set A⊂SdA\subset S^{d} of diameter strictly less than π\pi the restricted image f⁡(A)f(A) still is a Carathéodory subset. For a compact metric space XX with free ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action, we denote by cn​(X)c_{n}(X) the infimum over all t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty) such that, for any odd map f:X→ℝnf\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, there is a set A⊂XA\subset X with diameter bound diam⁡(A)≤t\mathrm{diam}(A)\leq t and with 0∈conv⁡(f⁡(A))0\in\mathrm{conv}(f(A)). We call cn​(X)c_{n}(X) the ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-Carathéodory number of XX. The Borsuk–Ulam theorem may be phrased as cd​(Sd)=0c_{d}(S^{d})=0. Upper bounds for cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}), for n>dn>d, follow easily from Theorem 2:

Corollary 4.1.

The ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-Carathéodory number of the dd-sphere satisfies the inequality

cn​(Sd)≤π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd).c_{n}(S^{d})\leq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}).
Proof.

Let f:Sd→ℝnf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} be a continuous odd map, and let δ=π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta=\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}). The map ff has a canonical continuous odd extension F:Sδd→ℝnF\colon S^{d}_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} defined by F⁡(μ)=∫Sdf​𝑑μF(\mu)=\int_{S^{d}}f\ d\mu. In addition, Theorem 2 gives a continuous odd map Sn→SδdS^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta}. By the Borsuk–Ulam theorem applied to the odd composition Sn→Sδd→ℝnS^{n}\to S^{d}_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, there exists some μ∈Sδd\mu\in S^{d}_{\delta} with 0=∫Sdf​𝑑μ0=\int_{S^{d}}f\ d\mu. Thus 0∈conv​{supp⁡(μ)}0\in\mathrm{conv}\{\mathrm{supp}(\mu)\} with diam⁡(supp⁡(μ))≤δ\mathrm{diam}(\mathrm{supp}(\mu))\leq\delta. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Corollary 4.1 substantially improves a result of the present authors in [3] that shows c2​k​d+2​d−1​(S2​d−1)≤2​π​k2​k+1c_{2kd+2d-1}(S^{2d-1})\leq\frac{2\pi k}{2k+1} (with equality in the case d=1d=1). For example, consider the projective code given by lines through the vertices of the hypercube: Let C⊂ℝdC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be the set of vectors whose coordinates are all ±1\pm 1. This is an antipodal set, C=−CC=-C, determining 2d−12^{d-1} lines through the origin. The angle between distinct lines is at least arccos⁡(1−1d)\arccos(1-\frac{1}{d}). Sr={x∈ℤd:‖x‖2=r​ and ​|xi|≤n​ for all ​i}.S_{r}=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}~:~\|x\|^{2}=r\text{ and }|x_{i}|\leq n\text{ for all }i\}.

Hence some SrS_{r} with 1≤r≤d​n21\leq r\leq dn^{2} has cardinality at least (2​n+1)d−1d​n2≥(2​n)dd​n2=2dd⋅ndn2>nd−2\frac{(2n+1)^{d}-1}{dn^{2}}\geq\frac{(2n)^{d}}{dn^{2}}=\frac{2^{d}}{d}\cdot\frac{n^{d}}{n^{2}}>n^{d-2}. For x,y∈Srx,y\in S_{r} with x≠±yx\neq\pm y the absolute value of the inner product |⟨x,y⟩||\langle x,y\rangle| is an integer and less than rr, in particular |⟨x,y⟩|≤r−1|\langle x,y\rangle|\leq r-1. Thus the angle between distinct lines determined by points in SrS_{r} is at least arccos⁡(1−1r)\arccos(1-\frac{1}{r}). It follows that pnd−2+1​(ℝ​Pd−1)≥arccos⁡(1−1d​n2)p_{n^{d-2}+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d-1})\geq\arccos(1-\frac{1}{dn^{2}}), and hence

cnd−2​(Sd−1)≤π−arccos⁡(1−1d​n2).c_{n^{d-2}}(S^{d-1})\leq\pi-\arccos\left(1-\frac{1}{dn^{2}}\right).

For a concrete example, recall that the 600600-cell (also known as the hypericosahedron or hexacosichoron) has 120120 centrally-symmetric vertices, which determine 6060 lines through the origin in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} with minimal angle π5\frac{\pi}{5}. Thus c59​(S3)≤π−π5c_{59}(S^{3})\leq\pi-\frac{\pi}{5} by Corollary 4.1, whereas our earlier bound (with d=2d=2 and k=14k=14) only gives c59​(S3)≤π−π29c_{59}(S^{3})\leq\pi-\frac{\pi}{29}.

Remark 4.3.

Instead of viewing Corollary 4.1 as an upper bound for cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}) in terms of pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}), equivalently pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)≤π−cn​(Sd)p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d})\leq\pi-c_{n}(S^{d}) gives an upper bound for projective codes in terms of zeros of odd maps. It remains an interesting open problem whether upper bounds for projective codes may be improved using this framework by exhibiting odd maps such that the image of sets up to a certain diameter may be separated from the origin. On the other hand, Theorem 3 shows that volume bounds for projective codes more generally provide upper bounds for the cohomological index of metric thickenings.

In much the same way that the Borsuk–Ulam theorem prohibits an embedding of SdS^{d} into ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, Corollary 4.1 gives bounds for how generic an embedding Sd↪ℝnS^{d}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}, n>dn>d, may be. Here the convex hulls of images of nearby points must intersect, where “nearby” is quantified by the distance of projective codes of size n+1n+1.

Corollary 4.4.

Let dd and nn be positive integers, and let δ≥cn​(Sd)\delta\geq c_{n}(S^{d}), which is satisfied if δ≥π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta\geq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}). Then for any map f:Sd→ℝnf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} there is a set X⊂SdX\subset S^{d} of diameter at most δ\delta such that the convex hulls of f⁡(X)f(X) and f⁡(−X)f(-X) intersect. Moreover, the preimages of the intersection point have the same coefficients with respect to XX and −X-X, that is, ∫Sdf⁡(x)​𝑑μ=∫Sdf⁡(−x)​𝑑μ\int_{S^{d}}f(x)\ d\mu=\int_{S^{d}}f(-x)\ d\mu for some μ∈Sδd\mu\in S^{d}_{\delta}.

By Carathéodory’s theorem, we may take XX to have size at most n+1n+1.

Proof.

Let δ≥cn​(Sd)\delta\geq c_{n}(S^{d}), which for example holds if δ≥π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta\geq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) by Corollary 4.1. Define F:Sδd→ℝnF\colon S^{d}_{\delta}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} by F⁡(μ)=∫Sd(f⁡(x)−f⁡(−x))​𝑑μ​(x)F(\mu)=\int_{S^{d}}(f(x)-f(-x))\ d\mu(x). The map FF is odd, and thus has a zero by the definition of the ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-Carathéodory number cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}). This implies ∫Sdf⁡(x)​𝑑μ​(x)=∫Sdf⁡(−x)​𝑑μ​(x)\int_{S^{d}}f(x)\ d\mu(x)=\int_{S^{d}}f(-x)\ d\mu(x) for some probability measure μ\mu on SdS^{d} whose support has diameter at most δ\delta. The point ∫Sdf⁡(x)​𝑑μ​(x)\int_{S^{d}}f(x)\ d\mu(x) lies in the convex hull of f⁡(X)f(X), where XX denotes the support μ\mu, while ∫Sdf⁡(−x)​𝑑μ​(x)∈conv​f​(−X)\int_{S^{d}}f(-x)\ d\mu(x)\in\mathrm{conv}\ f(-X). ∎

Example 4.5.

Let α\alpha be the common angle between the six (equiangular) lines in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} determined by the vertices of the icosahedron. That is, let ϕ=1+52\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2} be the golden ratio, and let α=arccos⁡(ϕ1+ϕ2)\alpha=\arccos(\frac{\phi}{1+\phi^{2}}). Corollary 4.4 shows that for any map f:S2→ℝ5f\colon S^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{5} there is a set X⊂S2X\subset S^{2} of diameter at most π−α\pi-\alpha such that conv​f​(X)∩conv​f​(−X)≠∅\mathrm{conv}\ f(X)\cap\mathrm{conv}\ f(-X)\neq\emptyset.

5. Topological bounds for the circular chromatic number

Lovász’s proof of Kneser’s conjecture [33] introduced topological lower bounds to the study of chromatic numbers of graphs. This classical result has been extended and adapted in various ways. For example, Simonyi and Tardos [42] proved topological lower bounds for the circular chromatic number of a graph.

Definition 5.1.

Given a graph GG with vertex set VV and edge set EE, an rr-circular coloring of GG is a map f:V→ℝ​P1f\colon V\to\mathbb{R}P^{1} such that d⁡(f⁡(v),f⁡(w))≥πrd(f(v),f(w))\geq\frac{\pi}{r} whenever (v,w)∈E(v,w)\in E. Recall that ℝ​P1\mathbb{R}P^{1} simply denotes the circle of circumference π\pi.

Definition 5.2.

The circular chromatic number of a graph GG is

χc​(G):=inf{r>0∣G​ is ​r​-circular colorable}.\chi_{c}(G):=\inf\{r>0\mid G\text{ is }r\text{-circular colorable}\}.

The infimum in the definition of the circular chromatic number of a graph GG is known to be attained if GG is finite. The topological lower bounds for χc​(G)\chi_{c}(G) are in terms of the topology of the box complex, which we define now. Let GG be a graph on vertex set {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\}. The box complex B0​(G)B_{0}(G) of GG is a simplicial complex on vertex set Q={1,…,n}∪{−1,…,−n}Q=\{1,\dots,n\}\cup\{-1,\dots,-n\}. A subset σ⊂Q\sigma\subset Q is a face of B0​(G)B_{0}(G) if for every v∈σv\in\sigma with v>0v>0 and every w∈σw\in\sigma with w<0w<0, the tuple (v,−w)(v,-w) forms an edge of GG. In particular, {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} and {−1,…,−n}\{-1,\dots,-n\} are faces of B0​(G)B_{0}(G). The complex B0​(G)B_{0}(G) has a free ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-action which swaps the vertices vv and −v-v and extends linearly to the faces of B0​(G)B_{0}(G). The box complex B0​(G)B_{0}(G) that we use is only one of several possible definitions; see for example [18, 36, 42] which study both the box complex B0​(G)B_{0}(G) along with variants thereof.

We can now state the result of Simonyi and Tardos:

Theorem 7 (Simonyi–Tardos [42, Theorem 6]).

Given a finite graph GG, if there is a continuous odd map S2​k−1→B0​(G)S^{2k-1}\to B_{0}(G), then χc​(G)≥2​k\chi_{c}(G)\geq 2k.

Here we show that Theorem 7 is a consequence of bounds for the topology of metric thickenings of the circle. Our proof in particular gives an explanation for the dependence of the bounds for the circular chromatic number on the parity of the coindex of B0​(G)B_{0}(G): When δ\delta exceeds a critical value when the index of the metric thickenings of the circle Sδ1S^{1}_{\delta} increases, the index in fact increases by two (see Lemma 2.2). Our proof of Theorem 7 is based on Theorem 8 and Lemmas 5.3–5.4, which we now provide.

Theorem 8.

Let GG be a finite graph with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and edge set E⁡(G)E(G), and let C​GCG denote the cone over GG with vertex set V⁡(C​G)=V⁡(G)∪{∙}V(CG)=V(G)\cup\{\bullet\} and edge set E⁡(C​G)=E⁡(G)∪{(∙,v)∣v∈V⁡(G)}E(CG)=E(G)\cup\{(\bullet,v)\mid v\in V(G)\}. If there is a continuous odd map S2​k→B0​(C​G)S^{2k}\to B_{0}(CG), then χc​(C​G)≥2​k+1\chi_{c}(CG)\geq 2k+1.

Proof.

Suppose GG is a finite graph with χc​(C​G)<2​k+1\chi_{c}(CG)<2k+1. Let the map f:V⁡(C​G)→ℝ​P1f\colon V(CG)\to\mathbb{R}P^{1} be given such that for some small ε>0\varepsilon>0 we have dℝ​P1​(f⁡(v),f⁡(w))≥π2​k+1+εd_{\mathbb{R}P^{1}}(f(v),f(w))\geq\frac{\pi}{2k+1}+\varepsilon whenever (v,w)∈E⁡(C​G)(v,w)\in E(CG). dS1​(F⁡(v),F⁡(∙))=π−dS1​(F⁡(v),−F⁡(∙))≤π−(π2​k+1+ε)=δ,d_{S^{1}}(F(v),F(\bullet))=\pi-d_{S^{1}}(F(v),-F(\bullet))\leq\pi-\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2k+1}+\varepsilon\right)=\delta, (1)

and similarly dS1(F(−v),F(−∙))≤δd_{S^{1}}(F(-v),F(-\bullet))\leq\delta. Lemma 5.3.

For a finite graph GG, χc​(G)≥χc​(C​G)−1\chi_{c}(G)\geq\chi_{c}(CG)-1.

Proof.

Let f:V⁡(G)→ℝ​P1f\colon V(G)\to\mathbb{R}P^{1} be a circular rr-coloring of GG. We need to construct a circular (r+1)(r+1)-coloring of C​GCG. Parametrize ℝ​P1\mathbb{R}P^{1} as [0,π][0,\pi] with 00 and π\pi identified into one point, which we will denote by x0x_{0}. Choose the parametrization in such a way that some vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) satisfies f⁡(v)=x0f(v)=x_{0}.

Now think of ff as a map f:V⁡(G)→[0,π)f\colon V(G)\to[0,\pi). Define a map g:V⁡(C​G)→[0,π)g\colon V(CG)\to[0,\pi) by g⁡(v)=rr+1​f​(v)g(v)=\frac{r}{r+1}f(v) for v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) and g⁡(∙)=rr+1​πg(\bullet)=\frac{r}{r+1}\pi. It is easily verified that gg is a circular (r+1)(r+1)-coloring of C​GCG. ∎

Lemma 5.4.

For a finite graph GG, coind⁡(B0​(C​G))≥coind⁡(B0​(G))+1\mathrm{coind}(B_{0}(CG))\geq\mathrm{coind}(B_{0}(G))+1.

Proof.

To prove the lemma, it is sufficient to prove that B0​(C​G)B_{0}(CG) is the suspension of B0​(G)B_{0}(G) (see, for instance, [42, Lemma 3.1]). Let GG have vertex set {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\}, and so B0​(G)B_{0}(G) has vertex set {1,…,n}∪{−1,…,−n}\{1,\dots,n\}\cup\{-1,\dots,-n\}. Note that the box complex B0​(C​G)B_{0}(CG) has two additional vertices that are not present in B0​(G)B_{0}(G), which we will denote by ∙\bullet and −⁣∙-\bullet. To prove that B0​(C​G)B_{0}(CG) is the suspension of B0​(G)B_{0}(G), we must verify that both σ∪{∙}\sigma\cup\{\bullet\} and σ∪{−∙}\sigma\cup\{-\bullet\} are faces of B0​(C​G)B_{0}(CG) for any given face σ\sigma of B0​(G)B_{0}(G). We do only the former, as the argument for the latter is nearly identical. Toward that end, for a given face σ∈B0​(G)\sigma\in B_{0}(G), consider any v∈σ∪{∙}v\in\sigma\cup\{\bullet\} with v>0v>0 and any w∈σ∪{∙}w\in\sigma\cup\{\bullet\} with w<0w<0 (which implies w≠∙w\neq\bullet). There are two possibilities: If v∈σv\in\sigma, we have (v,−w)∈E⁡(G)⊂E⁡(C​G)(v,-w)\in E(G)\subset E(CG) because σ∈B0​(G)\sigma\in B_{0}(G). Otherwise, if v=∙v=\bullet, we have (v,−w)=(∙,−w)∈E⁡(C​G)(v,-w)=(\bullet,-w)\in E(CG) by the definition of C​GCG. Hence σ∪{∙}\sigma\cup\{\bullet\} is a face of B0​(C​G)B_{0}(CG). ∎

We are prepared to prove Theorem 7.

Proof of Theorem 7.

Since there is a continuous odd map S2​k−1→B0​(G)S^{2k-1}\to B_{0}(G), we have coind⁡(B0​(G))≥2​k−1\mathrm{coind}(B_{0}(G))\geq 2k-1. So coind⁡(B0​(C​G))≥2​k\mathrm{coind}(B_{0}(CG))\geq 2k by Lemma 5.4, i.e. there is a continuous odd map S2​k→B0​(C​G)S^{2k}\to B_{0}(CG). Hence, Theorem 8 implies χc​(C​G)≥2​k+1\chi_{c}(CG)\geq 2k+1. Finally, by Lemma 5.3 we have χc​(G)≥χc​(C​G)−1≥(2​k+1)−1=2​k\chi_{c}(G)\geq\chi_{c}(CG)-1\geq(2k+1)-1=2k. ∎

6. Generalizations of the Ham Sandwich theorem

The Ham Sandwich theorem, originally conjectured by Steinhaus in the “Scottish book,” was proved by Banach and Stone–Tukey [43]. See [9] for the history of this result, including a note on Banach’s contribution to the proof in dimension 33.

Theorem 9 (Ham Sandwich theorem).

Let μ1,…,μd\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d} be finite Borel measures in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that every hyperplane has measure 00 for each of the μi\mu_{i}. Then there exists a hyperplane HH such that μi​(H+)=12​μi​(ℝd)\mu_{i}(H^{+})=\frac{1}{2}\mu_{i}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d, where H+H^{+} denotes one of the half-spaces defined by HH.

Informally, in the case of three measurable subsets of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, a sandwich made of three ingredients may be equipartitioned (that is, divided into two sandwiches each containing equal amounts of all three ingredients) using a single planar slice.

The Ham Sandwich theorem is perhaps the most well-known example of a mass partition theorem. In general, such theorems seek to establish the existence of families of partitions of Euclidean spaces splitting a given family of measures in a particular way. For example, Grünbaum [24] asked if it is always possible to divide a single mass in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} by dd hyperplanes to obtain 2d2^{d} equal parts. This question was answered in the affirmative by Hadwiger [26] for d≤3d\leq 3, but was proved to be false for d≥5d\geq 5 by Avis [8]. See [40, 19] for surveys of mass partition theorems and related results in combinatorial topology and combinatorial geometry, including Ham Sandwich-type theorems allowing multiple planar slices and theorems concerning the fair division of cakes and necklaces. There are versions of the Ham Sandwich theorem studying when one can bisect more masses than the dimension of the ambient space, for example including divisions by algebraic surfaces [43] or divisions of projections onto hyperplanes [41].

Theorem 1 and Corollary 4.4 allow us to extend the Ham Sandwich theorem to the setting in which the number of measures exceeds the dimension of the ambient space. For the purpose of illustration, we refer to the following as the “log bundle” theorem.

Informally, in the case of three measurable subsets of the disk, Theorem 10 says the following: Suppose a bundle of three logs needs to be divided up using equipment that permits only two kinds of cuts. First, we can perform “horizontal cuts,” perpendicular to the bundle (Figure 2 (left)), dividing the bundle up into shorter bundles. Secondly, through the centers of each resulting shorter bundles, we can perform a single “vertical cut” to produce two hemi-bundles (Figure 2 (right)). Furthermore, the blade used to perform each “vertical cut” is on a fixed pivot that cannot swivel by an angle of more than 2​π3\frac{2\pi}{3}. Then, in light of these constraints, it is always possible to obtain an equipartition of the bundle (that is, two piles of wood each containing exactly half the mass of each log) by selecting exactly one of each of the resulting hemi-bundles from each of the shorter bundles.

Theorem 10 (Generalization of Theorem 9).

Fix integers d,n≥1d,n\geq 1. Let

Dd+1={(x1,x2,…,xd+1,0)|x12+x22+⋯+xd+12≤1}⊂ℝd+2D^{d+1}=\{(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{d+1},0)~|~x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\dots+x_{d+1}^{2}\leq 1\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+2}

and suppose A1,…,An⊂Dd+1A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\subset D^{d+1} are measurable sets. For

p∈∂Dd+1={(x1,x2,…,xd+1,0)|x12+x22+⋯+xd+12=1},p\in\partial D^{d+1}=\{(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{d+1},0)~|~x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\cdots+x_{d+1}^{2}=1\},

let π⁡(p)={x∈ℝd+2|⟨x,p⟩=0}\pi(p)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d+2}~|~\langle x,p\rangle=0\} denote the hyperplane passing through the origin normal to pp. Furthermore, let H+​(p)H^{+}(p) and H−​(p)H^{-}(p) denote the (closed) halfspaces of ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2} determined by the inequalities ⟨x,p⟩≥0\langle x,p\rangle\geq 0 and ⟨x,p⟩≤0\langle x,p\rangle\leq 0, respectively. Then, there exist numbers 0=t0≤t1≤⋯≤tk≤tk+1=10=t_{0}\leq t_{1}\leq\cdots\leq t_{k}\leq t_{k+1}=1 with k≤nk\leq n and vectors p1,…,pk+1∈∂Dd+1p_{1},\dots,p_{k+1}\in\partial D^{d+1} such that

  1. (1)

    the vectors pip_{i} are “close” in the sense that arccos⁡(⟨pi,pj⟩)≤π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\arccos(\langle p_{i},p_{j}\rangle)\leq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) for all ii and jj (in particular, no two vectors are antipodal), and

  2. (2)

    there exists an equipartition of the nn masses Aj×IA_{j}\times I given by taking (Aj×[ti−1,ti])∩H+​(pi)(A_{j}\times[t_{i-1},t_{i}])\cap H^{+}(p_{i}) for each 1≤i≤k+11\leq i\leq k+1.

This equipartition means that for each jj, the sum of the measures of (Aj×[ti−1,ti])∩H+​(pi)(A_{j}\times[t_{i-1},t_{i}])\cap H^{+}(p_{i}) is equal to the sum of the measures of (Aj×[ti−1,ti])∩H−​(pi)(A_{j}\times[t_{i-1},t_{i}])\cap H^{-}(p_{i}), where both sums vary over 1≤i≤k+11\leq i\leq k+1.

Proof.

Define a continuous function f:Sd→ℝnf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} by

p↦(the measure of ​A1∩H+​(p),…,the measure of ​An∩H+​(p)).p\mapsto\left(\text{the measure of }A_{1}\cap H^{+}(p),\dots,\text{the measure of }A_{n}\cap H^{+}(p)\right).

By Corollary 4.4 there exist vectors p1,…,pk+1∈Sdp_{1},\dots,p_{k+1}\in S^{d} (with k≤nk\leq n by Carathéodory’s theorem) and convex coefficients λ1,λ2,…​λk+1\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots\lambda_{k+1} such that arccos⁡(⟨pi,pj⟩)≤π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\arccos(\langle p_{i},p_{j}\rangle)\leq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) for all ii and jj and

∑i=1k+1λi​f​(pi)=∑i=1k+1λi​f​(−pi).\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_{i}f(p_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_{i}f(-p_{i}).

Observe that

f⁡(−p)=(the measure of ​A1∩H−​(p),…,the measure of ​An∩H−​(p)).f(-p)=(\text{the measure of }A_{1}\cap H^{-}(p),\ \dots,\ \text{the measure of }A_{n}\cap H^{-}(p)).

Setting ti=∑j=1iλjt_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\lambda_{j} for each 0≤i≤k+10\leq i\leq k+1 completes the proof. ∎

Remark 6.1.

We may obtain a stronger version of Theorem 10, allowing one more set to be equipartitioned, by dropping the requirement that each hyperplane π⁡(p)\pi(p) must pass through the origin. In this setting, n+1n+1 sets may be equipartitioned by n+1n+1 hyperplanes determined by vectors p1,…,pn+1p_{1},\dots,p_{n+1} which again satisfy arccos⁡(⟨pi,pj⟩)≤π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\arccos(\langle p_{i},p_{j}\rangle)\leq\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) for all ii and jj.

We will refer to a hyperplane that passes through the origin as a linear hyperplane. A linear hyperplane HH is oriented if the two halfspaces determined by HH come with a choice of positive halfspace H+H^{+} and negative halfspace H−H^{-}. The Ham Sandwich theorem may be restated in the following way:

Theorem 11 (Ham Sandwich theorem – restated).

Let μ1,…,μd\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d} be finite Borel measures on Sd⊂ℝd+1S^{d}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1} such that every linear hyperplane in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} has measure 00 for each of the μi\mu_{i}. Then there exists a linear hyperplane HH in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} such that μi​(H+∩Sd)=12​μi​(Sd)\mu_{i}(H^{+}\cap S^{d})=\frac{1}{2}\mu_{i}(S^{d}) for i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d, where H+H^{+} denotes one of the half-spaces defined by HH.

Theorem 1 implies the following:

Theorem 12.

Let μ1,…,μn\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{n} on Sd⊂ℝd+1S^{d}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1} be finite Borel measures such that each linear hyperplane in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} has measure 00 for each of the μi\mu_{i}. Then there exists a set ℋ\mathcal{H} of oriented linear hyperplanes in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} at pairwise angle (in ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d}) at most δ=π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta=\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) such that, for each ii, at least half of μi\mu_{i} is contained in the negative halfspace determined by some hyperplane in ℋ\mathcal{H}, and at least half of μi\mu_{i} is contained in the positive halfspace determined by some hyperplane in ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Proof.

For x∈Sd⊂ℝd+1x\in S^{d}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, let H−​(x)H^{-}(x) and H+​(x)H^{+}(x) denote the (closed) halfspaces of ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} determined by the inequalities ⟨y,x⟩≤0\langle y,x\rangle\leq 0 and ⟨y,x⟩≥0\langle y,x\rangle\geq 0, respectively. Let VV denote the vector space of odd maps Sd→ℝS^{d}\to\mathbb{R} generated by the vectors fif_{i} defined by fi​(x)=μi​(H+​(x))−μi​(H−​(x))f_{i}(x)=\mu_{i}(H^{+}(x))-\mu_{i}(H^{-}(x)) for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Note that VV has dimension at most nn, and that each fif_{i} is odd. By Theorem 1, there exists a set A⊂SdA\subset S^{d} of diameter at most δ\delta such that, for every f∈Vf\in V, the restriction f|Af|_{A} is not strictly positive (and, since −f∈V-f\in V, it is also true that the restriction f|Af|_{A} is not strictly negative). Hence, for each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, there must exist points ai,bi∈Aa_{i},b_{i}\in A such that fi​(ai)f_{i}(a_{i}) is nonpositive and fi​(bi)f_{i}(b_{i}) is nonnegative, that is, at least half of μi\mu_{i} is contained in the negative halfspace H−​(ai)H^{-}(a_{i}) and at least half of μi\mu_{i} is contained in the positive halfspace H+​(bi)H^{+}(b_{i}). So we are done by letting ℋ={H±​(a):a∈A}\mathcal{H}=\{H^{\pm}(a)~:~a\in A\}. ∎

Remark 6.2.

Instead of δ=π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\delta=\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) we could have phrased both Theorem 10 and Theorem 12 for the smallest δ\delta such that the metric thickening SδdS^{d}_{\delta} has cohomological index at least nn. For n=dn=d, this δ\delta is zero, since SdS^{d} is a subspace of SδdS^{d}_{\delta} for any δ≥0\delta\geq 0. In the case n=dn=d and δ=0\delta=0, the stronger version of Theorem 10 described in Remark 6.1 specializes to Theorem 9, and Theorem 12 specializes to Theorem 11.

7. Generalizations of Lyusternik–Shnirel’man–Borsuk covering theorems

Theorem 13 (Lyusternik–Shnirel’man–Borsuk covering theorem [34]).

For any cover A1,…,Ad+1A_{1},\dots,A_{d+1} of the sphere SdS^{d} by d+1d+1 closed sets, there is at least one set containing a pair of antipodal points.

In fact, the conclusion of Theorem 13 holds for more general collections of subsets of SdS^{d}.

Theorem 14.

For any cover A1,…,Ad+1A_{1},\dots,A_{d+1} of the sphere SdS^{d} by d+1d+1 sets such that the first dd sets A1,…,AdA_{1},\dots,A_{d} are each open or closed, there is at least one set containing a pair of antipodal points.

A proof of this theorem appears in [6]; see also [21, 35]. We now consider a generalization in which the number of sets in the covering may be arbitrarily large with respect to the dimension of the sphere.

Theorem 15 (Generalization of Theorem 14).

Fix integers n≥d≥1n\geq d\geq 1 and suppose A1,…,An+1A_{1},\dots,A_{n+1} is a cover of the sphere SdS^{d} by n+1n+1 sets such that the first nn sets A1,…,AnA_{1},\dots,A_{n} are each open or closed. Furthermore, suppose that any subset of the sphere of diameter at most cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}) is contained in some subset AiA_{i}. In particular, this is satisfied if every subset of the sphere of diameter at most π−pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)\pi-p_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d}) is contained in some AiA_{i}. Then, there is at least one set AiA_{i} containing a pair of antipodal points.

Recall the ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-Carathéodory number cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}) is defined as the infimum over all t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty) such that for any odd map f:X→ℝnf\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^{n} there is a set A⊂XA\subset X with diam⁡(A)≤t\mathrm{diam}(A)\leq t and 0∈conv⁡(f⁡(A))0\in\mathrm{conv}(f(A)). The above theorem generalizes Theorem 13 because if n=dn=d, then the condition that any subset of the sphere of diameter at most cd​(Sd)=0c_{d}(S^{d})=0 is in some subset AiA_{i} simply implies that the sets AiA_{i} cover the sphere.

Proof.

Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that no set in the cover contains antipodal points. Consider the continuous map f:Sd→ℝ≥0nf\colon S^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n} defined by f⁡(x)=(d⁡(x,A1),…,d⁡(x,An))f(x)=(d(x,A_{1}),\ldots,d(x,A_{n})), where d⁡(x,Ai)=infy∈Ai{d⁡(x,y)}d(x,A_{i})=\inf_{y\in A_{i}}\{d(x,y)\}. By Corollary 4.4, there exists a subset {x1,…,xm}⊂Sd\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\}\subset S^{d} (with m≤n+1m\leq n+1) of diameter at most cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}) and convex coefficients λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 such that

y:=∑i=1mλi​f​(xi)=∑i=1mλi​f​(−xi).y:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}f(x_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}f(-x_{i}). (2)

Since An+1A_{n+1} does not contain antipodal points by assumption, for each 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m at least one of xix_{i} and −xi-x_{i} must be contained in some element of {A1,…,An}\{A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\}. In fact, we claim that there must exist a single Aj∈{A1,…,An}A_{j}\in\{A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\} containing all of {x1,…,xm}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\} or all of {−x1,…,−xm}\{-x_{1},\dots,-x_{m}\}. Toward proving the claim, note that the points x1,…,xmx_{1},\dots,x_{m} are all contained in some element of the cover because diam⁡({x1,…,xm})≤cn​(Sd)\mathrm{diam}(\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\})\leq c_{n}(S^{d}). Hence, either {x1,…,xm}⊆Aj\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}\subseteq A_{j} for some 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, or {x1,…,xm}⊆An+1\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}\subseteq A_{n+1}. In the latter case, because An+1A_{n+1} does not contain antipodal points, we have {−x1,…,−xm}⊆Sd∖An+1\{-x_{1},\dots,-x_{m}\}\subseteq S^{d}\setminus A_{n+1}. Then, because diam⁡({−x1,…,−xm})=diam⁡({x1,…,xm})\mathrm{diam}(\{-x_{1},\dots,-x_{m}\})=\mathrm{diam}(\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}), it follows that {−x1,…,−xm}⊆Aj\{-x_{1},\dots,-x_{m}\}\subseteq A_{j} for some 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n. This proves the claim.

Now, observe that either d⁡(xi,Aj)=0d(x_{i},A_{j})=0 for all 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m or d⁡(−xi,Aj)=0d(-x_{i},A_{j})=0 for all 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m. Furthermore, by considering the jthj^{\text{th}} coordinate of yy in Equation (2) above, it follows that both d⁡(xi,Aj)=0d(x_{i},A_{j})=0 and d⁡(−xi,Aj)=0d(-x_{i},A_{j})=0 for all ii. There are two cases:

  1. (1)

    Suppose AjA_{j} is closed. In this case, d⁡(xi,Aj)=0d(x_{i},A_{j})=0 and d⁡(−xi,Aj)=0d(-x_{i},A_{j})=0 imply that {xi,−xi}⊆Aj\{x_{i},-x_{i}\}\subseteq A_{j} for all ii, contradicting the assumption that no set in the cover contains antipodal points.

  2. (2)

    Suppose AjA_{j} is open. Note that d⁡(−xi,Aj)=0d(-x_{i},A_{j})=0 implies −xi∈Aj¯-x_{i}\in\overline{A_{j}} for all ii. In turn, Aj¯\overline{A_{j}} is contained in the closed set Sn∖(−Aj)⊇AjS^{n}\setminus(-A_{j})\supseteq A_{j}. Hence, each −xi-x_{i} belongs to Sn∖(−Aj)S^{n}\setminus(-A_{j}), which implies that xi∉Ajx_{i}\notin A_{j} for all ii. Swapping the roles of xix_{i} and −xi-x_{i}, a similar argument shows that −xi∉Aj-x_{i}\notin A_{j} for all ii. This contradicts the fact that AjA_{j} contains all of {x1,…,xm}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\} or all of {−x1,…,−xm}\{-x_{1},\dots,-x_{m}\}.

Hence some AjA_{j} for 1≤j≤n+11\leq j\leq n+1 contains a pair of antipodal points. ∎

8. Conclusion

The presence of a large projective code bounds the topology of the metric thickening of a sphere, which in turn controls the structure of zeros of odd maps from the sphere into Euclidean space. As a consequence, we obtain a generalization of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem for maps from spheres into higher-dimensional codomains. We derive consequences of this Borsuk–Ulam theorem for overdetermined versions of the Ham Sandwich theorem (more measures than the ambient dimension), for overdetermined versions of the Lyusternik–Shnirel’man–Borsuk covering theorem (more sets than the ambient dimension), for generic manifold embeddings, and for bounds on circular chromatic numbers.

We end with open questions on the topology of metric thickenings of spheres, their concrete relation to the size of projective codes, and on a possible connection to Gromov–Hausdorff distances between spheres.

Question 8.1.

Corollary 3.2 asserts that for any δ>π2\delta>\frac{\pi}{2}, there is an arbitrarily large jump in coindex between Sπ/2d≃SdS^{d}_{\pi/2}\simeq S^{d} and SδdS^{d}_{\delta} for dd sufficiently large. Is it possible to determine coind⁡(Sδd)\mathrm{coind}(S^{d}_{\delta}) and ind⁡(Sδd)\mathrm{ind}(S^{d}_{\delta}) as a function of δ∈(π2,π)\delta\in(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi) at least asymptotically in dd?

Question 8.2.

Theorem 2 shows if pn+1​(ℝ​Pd)≥π−δp_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}P^{d})\geq\pi-\delta then ind⁡(Sδd)≥coind⁡(Sδd)≥n\mathrm{ind}(S^{d}_{\delta})\geq\mathrm{coind}(S^{d}_{\delta})\geq n. Does an approximate converse of this result hold?

We only raise the question about an “approximate” converse, since SδdS^{d}_{\delta} in addition to the size of codes in ℝ​Pd\mathbb{R}P^{d} also encodes symmetries of SdS^{d}. For example, an equilateral triangle inscribed in ℝ​P1\mathbb{R}P^{1} gives a projective code with distance π3\frac{\pi}{3}. For δ=π−π3\delta=\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}, Theorem 2 then gives an odd map S2→Sδ1S^{2}\to S^{1}_{\delta}. However, Sδ1≃S3S^{1}_{\delta}\simeq S^{3}, since there are a circle’s worth of equilateral triangles in ℝ​P1\mathbb{R}P^{1}.

Question 8.3.

For d≤nd\leq n, could the ℤ/2\mathbb{Z}/2-Carathéodory number cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}) be equal to 2⋅dGH​(Sd,Sn)2\cdot d_{\mathrm{GH}}(S^{d},S^{n}), twice the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between the spheres SdS^{d} and SnS^{n}, equipped with the geodesic metric? This is known to be true when n≤3n\leq 3, and is consistent with known bounds on cn​(Sd)c_{n}(S^{d}) (see [14, Table page 80]) and on dGH​(Sd,Sn)d_{\mathrm{GH}}(S^{d},S^{n}) (see [32, Figure 2]). Or does one quantity bound the other?
